paragraphs: Oregon State University's special collections describe Alice Biddle as a member of the college's first graduating class in 1870. She finished the curriculum in three years and graduated at 16. The university chronology says that class was one woman and two men, Alice Biddle, J.K.P. Currin, and Robert M. Veatch, and that these were the first degrees granted in the western United States by a state-assisted college or university. At the June 30 commencement she read a paper, "Progress of Mind." In December 1870 she married professor William W. Moreland.

The formal title of the 1983 bronze is The Quest, and the artist is Kirk St. Maur. Beaver's Digest places the figure on the busy path between Memorial Union and Strand Agriculture Hall and says she holds a diploma. The university's exhibit record places the sculpture at the southwest corner of Strand Agricultural Hall. A plaque quoted in the campus article says the work reflects the energy, dedication, and strength of all students in the pursuit of learning.

Wikipedia, citing the Smithsonian inventory, describes a standing bronze about 5 feet 11 inches by 4 feet by 4 feet 6 inches. Her head turns to her right, and her proper right hand holds a rolled paper. The skirt is signed with the artist's name, a copyright mark, and 1983. The nearby marker says she became, in 1870, the first woman to graduate from what is now Oregon State University. The Oregon Arts Commission commissioned the sculpture under the 1% for Art in State Buildings program, and the university administers it.

paragraphs: The U.S. Forest Service describes Amanda's Trail as a descent from Cape Perpetua through coastal woodland to a grotto with a concrete statue. The trail and statue remember Amanda, a woman of the Coos Tribe who was forcibly marched to the Alsea Sub-agency camp in the 1860s. The City of Yachats calls her a blind Coos woman who suffered injustices during the reservation years. Oregon Hikers identifies her as Amanda De Cuys and says a 1864 detachment of the 4th California Infantry, led by Lt. Louis Herzer, took people north to the Alsea Sub-agency at Yachats. She had been living with a white man and had a daughter who stayed with her father. Her fate is unknown.

Joanne Kittel's short history of the trail says ranger Loyd Collett named the route for Amanda in the 1980s after reading that she was forced to march barefoot over Cape Perpetua. George Copage donated Sy Meadow's statue in 2003. A December 2015 mudslide destroyed that statue and the bridge. One of three statues Meadow made was donated and installed in a more secure spot in 2016. The current high-level suspension bridge opened in 2022. Oregon Hikers calls the figure on the trail the second statue and says a sign warns that it carries a tracking device. Offerings such as necklaces are often left on it.

From the south end of Yachats Ocean Road the city calls the walk to the statue a moderate hike of about 1 mile. The full trail is 3.2 miles one way to the Cape Perpetua lookout, and bikes are not allowed. The Forest Service lists the trail as 2.9 miles and moderate to difficult when started from the Cape Perpetua day-use area, where a day-use fee or recreation pass is required. The New Year's Day Peace Hike, a 4.5-mile round trip from Yachats to the gathering area, began in 2012. Kittel writes that it now draws more than 200 people and includes tribal representatives.

paragraphs: Travel Oregon, using a Sisters Chamber listing, says Barclay Park is in downtown Sisters and is named for Harold and Dorothy Barclay. The Nugget Newspaper, reporting Dorothy Barclay's death in April 2003, said the city had named a new downtown park on Ash Street the Harold and Dorothy Barclay Memorial Park for the couple's contributions. Harold pushed the town's Western architectural theme as Sisters shifted from logging toward tourism, and the Barclays developed Barclay Square on Cascade Avenue.

The park's best-known sculpture is a bronze great blue heron. The Nugget reported that family and friends gathered in the park on Saturday, December 8, 2012, to dedicate the 10-foot figure in memory of Elizabeth Dasch, an artist and longtime resident who died in 2009 at 97. Local sculptor Danae Bennett Miller built it from 70 pieces of bronze welded around a stainless steel frame. Dasch's three children gave $25,000. The plaque reads: "She loved all the birds, Especially the Cranes and Herons. Artist: Danae Bennett Miller. Dedicated: December 8, 2012. Given to the City of Sisters In Memory of Elizabeth Dasch By her Family and Friends."

The City of Sisters public-art list also places a mural by Jerry Werner in Barclay Park, installed in May 2004, and a Welcome to Sisters mural by Karen Eland and Katie Daisy, installed in May 2022. The heron itself is listed as installed in December 2012. Mayor Lon Kellstrom, at the heron dedication, tied the piece to a run of public art the city had gained in those years.

paragraphs: The Black Bird store says Lee Hobbs founded it in 1965 as an army surplus store. The giant bird out front was fashioned after a 10-foot magpie at Yard Birds in Centralia, Washington, a store owned by a friend of Hobbs. The store's own account says Hobbs designed and built the 29-foot bird from rebar, hog wire, and fiberglass. Staff dress it in a tank top and shorts for the Pear Blossom Run and in a Santa hat and candy cane at Christmas.

The Oregonian, in a May 2022 feature, describes bulging biceps, toes that curl upward, and claws that bend at opposing angles. The arms are roughly twice the length of the legs. The open beak looks down on drivers from two concrete pillars painted B.B. Hobbs had worked as a fabricator at Boeing and as a mechanic. Southern Oregon Historical Society says concrete bars formed the skeleton, hog wire was clipped over the frame, and fiberglass was sprayed on. It puts the underpinning 30 feet below the surface and says the yellow-and-black head was wired with a speaker. The bird had three talons on each hand and two on each foot.

Hobbs died in 1973. The Oregonian says he was 51 and died of lung cancer, and that longtime employee Bill Quitt later became president. In 2021 the store hired Augie's Fiberglass to repair and repaint the bird after decades of weather and the occasional car rear-ending. A speaker in the beak had stopped working. A smaller Black Bird store later opened in Phoenix. The Medford address published by the store is 1810 W. Main Street, Medford, OR 97501.

paragraphs: Wikipedia describes Joan of Arc, also called Joan of Arc, Maiden of Orleans, as an outdoor copy of Emmanuel Fremiet's 1874 gilded bronze Jeanne d'Arc at the Place des Pyramides in Paris. Henry Waldo Coe, who had seen the Paris statue, donated Portland's copy. It arrived from France in 1924 and was dedicated on Memorial Day, May 30, 1925, for the doughboys of World War I. It was one of four statues Coe gave the city. It stands in Coe Circle at Northeast Cesar E. Chavez Boulevard, formerly 39th, and Glisan, in Laurelhurst.

The same account, citing the Smithsonian inventory, says the bronze measures about 12 by 5.5 by 9 feet, the flag is copper, and the granite base is about 8 by 3 by 9 feet. A Regional Arts and Culture Council catalog lists the work as bronze, copper, and gold leaf, dated 1924, with a height of 13 feet. That catalog says a dedication on May 30, 1925, included remarks from President Calvin Coolidge and French President Gaston Doumergue. Wikipedia says Margaret Goodin Fritsch won the contest for the base design.

Gold leaf wore away over the years. The sculpture was surveyed by the Smithsonian's Save Outdoor Sculpture program in 1993. In 2002, after a $24,000 grant and other fundraising, the city restored the gold leaf and replaced the pennant in Joan's right hand and the laurel wreath on her head. The arts council says the sculpture was rededicated in May 2002 after nearly three years of planning, with support from a Save Outdoor Sculpture grant, Target, the National Endowment for the Arts, Providence Health Systems, and neighbors.

paragraphs: The City of Portland's building-project page calls Portlandia the city's largest sculpture and the second-largest copper repousse statue in the country, after the Statue of Liberty. If she were standing, the city says, she would be 50 feet tall. In 1981 the city held a national competition for a sculpture at the new Portland Building. Architect Michael Graves wanted a large Lady Commerce, the woman on the city seal. In 1982 the Arts Commission chose Raymond Kaskey's design. He modeled the figure on his wife. The work took three years and at least 50 hammer strokes per square inch. The 6.5-ton sculpture floated up the Willamette on October 6, 1985.

The Portland Tribune's notes for the 30th birthday in 2015 match the height, 34 feet 10 inches, the weight, 6.5 tons, and the makeup, a steel frame covered in hammered copper. paragraphs: The Bulletin's 2022 park-art tour says Greg Congleton crafted Two Bits in 2011 as a tribute to Bend's logging history. paragraphs: This monument is in Marietta, Ohio, not in West Virginia. The Start Westward Memorial Society says Gutzon Borglum, the Mount Rushmore sculptor, visited Marietta in October 1936 and agreed to sculpt the memorial as a favor to former Ohio governor George White. He designed it in 1937 at his San Antonio studio, made a full-scale plaster, and worked with Ohio state architect John Schooley on the esplanade. A smaller clay model went to Marietta for the stone carvers. The society quotes the idea that Marietta was "the stepping stone, the first footprint of the nation as she started on her westward march."

The memorial was carved from local sandstone to employ local workers with New Deal WPA funds. On December 13, 1937, Borglum viewed the 80-ton block from which six heroic figures were carved. Carving began at a quarry near old Ohio River Lock 18. On May 7, 1938, the partly carved block, then 25 tons, was hauled to Muskingum Park. Schooley turned the standing pioneers to face Front Street so the boat faces the riverbank. Living New Deal says the group commemorates the first permanent American settlement in the Northwest Territory, in 1788, and that the memorial also includes a landing esplanade and four pylons topped with eagles.

Roosevelt arrived by train at 9 a.m. on July 8, 1938, and dedicated the memorial at 10 a.m. He closed with, "I hereby dedicate this great monument commemorating one hundred and fifty years of Americanism." Living New Deal says Borglum did not attend because he disagreed with executing the sculpture in sandstone rather than bronze. That page, updated in June 2023, said a project was underway to make a bronze replica and keep the sandstone original indoors. The catalog path for this record is under West Virginia. paragraphs: Scouting magazine says that on May 27, 1950, nearly 1,000 Boy Scouts marched through downtown Cheyenne to the capitol grounds to dedicate an eight-foot replica of the Statue of Liberty. Governor Arthur Crane spoke. The statues were part of the Boy Scouts' 40th-anniversary theme, "Strengthen the Arm of Liberty." Between 1949 and 1952, Scouts dedicated more than 200 copper figures, often called Little Sisters of Liberty, in 39 states and in Guam, Puerto Rico, the Canal Zone, and the Philippines. Jack P. Whitaker of Kansas City originated the project. Friedley-Voshardt of Chicago made the stamped-copper replicas, each with more than 40 sheets of copper and a wooden frame. Troops bought them for a reported $300 to $350.

The Cheyenne statue later stood at the state Supreme Court. Wyoming Tribune Eagle reported on April 11, 2008, that Eagle Scout Leland Duck and his father, Ron, recast the damaged copper figure in bronze rather than repair it. The copper one weighed about 60 pounds and the bronze about 400. Leland raised about $2,500 and the city contributed $6,000. Parks director Rick Parish said the statue would be the centerpiece of Law and Liberty Square in north Lions Park, across Lions Park Drive and northeast of the municipal pool, with historic documents in granite around it.

A 2012 transcription of the plaques, published from Troop 101's research, places the figure in Lions Park near Central Avenue, U.S. 85, and Kennedy Road, across the street northeast from the swimming pool. The plaque text includes the 1950 dedication line and "Statue of Liberty recast in bronze, Leland James Duck, Eagle Scout project, Troop 101, February 21, 2005," plus a 2008 Law and Liberty Plaza inscription. Statue of Liberty Worldwide lists a Boy Scout statue in Lions Park in Cheyenne and describes the series as about 100-inch stamped-copper replicas. The figure in the park today is the bronze recast, not the 1950 copper shell.

paragraphs: The American Heritage Center says the bronze Benjamin Franklin stands on the lawn south of the Arts and Sciences Building at the University of Wyoming. The idea began in 1955, ahead of the 250th anniversary of Franklin's birth. Professor and sculptor Robert Russin joined rancher and oilman Warren Richardson. Richardson and his siblings Clarence and Valeria wanted the statue on the campus. In a February 18, 1956, letter to President George Duke Humphrey, Richardson called Franklin a guiding inspiration for the youth of Wyoming. On March 9 the trustees accepted $17,500 from the family.

Russin had already made a model. The seven-foot bronze rests on a large polished granite base. After looking at several sites, the trustees chose the lawn south of the Arts and Sciences Building, later remembered as the site of Peanut Pond, which was filled in during 1962. The statue was installed on April 1, 1957, and formally dedicated on May 24. Russin told the ceremony that Franklin was a student all his life and quoted him: "The doors of wisdom are never shut."

The center calls this the first statue of Benjamin Franklin erected west of the Mississippi River. A campus newspaper satire just after the installation complained that the inscription listed scientist, man of letters, economist, and politician, and left out printer and journalist. A 2010 sculpture-tour checklist from the university art museum also places Russin's Ben Franklin south of the College of Arts and Sciences. A claim that only four standing Franklin statues exist worldwide was not on these pages.

paragraphs: Cowboy State Daily reported on June 11, 2023, that drivers on U.S. Highway 14/16/20 toward Yellowstone's east entrance had been passing the Wapiti Big Boy for about a decade. The figure stands on a concrete pedestal in a field about 20 miles west of Cody, smiling and holding a giant burger. James Geier, who owns the statue and the land, said he put it there on purpose in 2013. It is an authentic Big Boy rescued from a California restaurant. He took it down in 2020 for paint, and people thought it had been stolen. Roadside America says it appeared in the summer of 2013, some distance from the road in a fenced field, and lists admission as free for a view from the highway.

The Cody Enterprise reported on October 12, 2026, that Big Boy had returned the previous Saturday night to the pedestal on the south side of the North Fork Highway in Wapiti. For a short time a Captain Morgan figure, a promotional pirate that had been in Geier's barn about 15 years, stood in his place. The sheriff's office called to ask if the statue had been vandalized. Geier said locals give directions as "two miles past Big Boy on the right." The Wyoming Office of Tourism once used a photo of him, with Sheep Mountain behind, on its That's WY site.

The statue is on private land. The Enterprise says hunting is not allowed on the property. Geier's other works in the same field include Shadow, a rebar stallion, metal trees, and a metal moose he hides in the trees during hunting season so drivers will not shoot at it. paragraphs: The Shoshone National Forest says Dead Indian Summit Overlook is on the pass at 8,071 feet, with vistas of the Absaroka Mountains, the Beartooth range to the north, and the Clarks Fork River below, which the forest page identifies as a Wild and Scenic River. Interpretive signs cover the Nez Perce route and the surrounding ranges. The site is open 24 hours, no fee is required, parking is ample, and there is a vault toilet. There is no garbage collection.

Wikipedia places Dead Indian Pass at the same elevation on Wyoming Highway 296, on the Chief Joseph Scenic Byway, crossing the Absaroka Range in Park County. It associates the pass with the Nez Perce flight in the 1877 war. Pursued by troops under General O. O. Howard, the group reached the pass on September 8, 1877, saw soldiers below, feinted south, and then used Dead Indian Gulch to reach the Clarks Fork. Wikipedia gives two naming accounts: a Nez Perce killed near the pass in 1877, or a Bannock killed in 1878 by Crow scouts with Colonel Nelson A. Miles. Both are reported as accounts, not as a settled fact.

paragraphs: Travel Wyoming says the Herrick brothers, Ralph and Doug, first combined a taxidermied jackrabbit and deer antlers in Douglas in 1934. The original mount was stolen from a Douglas hotel in the late 1970s. Another version is at the Wyoming Pioneer Museum. During the state's 100th anniversary of statehood in 1990, residents dedicated Jackalope Square in the center of town. An eight-foot jackalope stands over a pavilion and lawn. The town square hosts a summer block party and a farmers market. Travel Wyoming says the town has been dubbed Jackalope City, and it points visitors to the Douglas Railroad Museum and Visitor Center for a comic hunting license limited to June 31, from midnight to 2 a.m.

The City of Douglas tells the same 1934 shop story: after a rabbit hunt, a dead rabbit landed next to deer antlers, and Ralph and Douglas Herrick went into the business of mounting jackrabbits with antlers. The city says Douglas was calling itself the Jackalope Capital of the World by the late 1940s. It also says the state trademarked the jackalope in 1965 and designated it in 1985. Those lines are the city's own. The same page separates the joke natural history, whiskey, milk, and lightning, from the taxidermy history.

The city says statues stand in downtown Jackalope Square and at the visitors center, and a 13-foot cutout is on a hillside near the north entrance from Interstate 25. Jackalope Days is each June. The city's street address, 101 N. Fourth Street, is city hall, not a published address for the square, so it is not used as the statue's address.

paragraphs: The Cheyenne Frontier Days Foundation says Wyoming artist D. Michael Thomas created the Just LeDoux It memorial bronze. It was dedicated in 2021 on opening day of the 125th Cheyenne Frontier Days, the year the event was dedicated to LeDoux. LeDoux was a world-champion bareback rider who competed in the arena and played the main stage. The statue shows those two sides of his career. It stands on the west side of Frontier Park, facing Hynds Boulevard.

The Wyoming Tribune Eagle, on June 22, 2021, watched the statue arrive. Thomas guided the 12.5-foot-tall, 17-foot-long bronze as a crane set it on a new pedestal at the southwest corner of the park. It is visible from Interstate 25 and faces the park-and-ride drop-off on Hynds Boulevard, just south of the large Frontier Days sign. The figure wears contestant number 125. Both this statue and Thomas's earlier one in Kaycee show LeDoux on Stormy Weather, the horse he rode at the 1976 National Finals Rodeo when he won the world title. In Cheyenne the bronze guitar leans against the base. Brian O'Leary hauled it from Caleco Foundry in Cody, where it was cast.

General chairman Jimmy Dean Siler said that year's celebration would honor LeDoux because he grew up in Cheyenne, stayed in Wyoming, won a world bareback title, and became a country headliner. The unveiling was planned for mid-July, before Frontier Days opened on July 23. A hometown paper's later "about 13 feet" and "2,000 pounds" were not on a page that loaded, so the measurements used here are the Tribune Eagle's, taken when the bronze was lifted into place.

paragraphs: The Cheyenne and Laramie County public-art record says the Robert Burns monument is a bronze of Burns in the costume of his time. It stands 6.5 feet high on a pedestal of Georgia gray granite 12.5 feet high. Scottish sculptor Henry Snell Gamley made it. Mary Gilchrist, widow of a Wyoming cattleman and a native of Ayrshire, Scotland, donated it to the city in 1929. The same record says Gamley died a year before the bronze was unveiled in November 1929 in Gilchrist Park, at the corner of Randall and Pioneer avenues. It gives the location as 2610 Pioneer Avenue, Cheyenne, WY 82001.

The Wyoming State Archives finding aid says the statue was dedicated on November 11, 1929, and that Mary Gilchrist funded the project. She was born in Scotland in 1840, joined her husband Andrew in America in 1869, and settled in Cheyenne in 1875. Andrew died in 1894. Mary died in January 1931 and is buried with him in Lakeview Cemetery. She gave the statue to the city in honor of her native Scotland. The archives place it in the small triangular park at Randall Avenue, Pioneer Avenue, and 26th Street. The subject index lists Robert Burns, 1759-1796, and Gamley, 1865-1928.

A Smithsonian inventory page that would add the foundry mark and the architect's name did not load, so those details are left out. The public-art page spells Gamley's middle name once as Gamely and once as Gamley. The archives use Henry Snell Gamley.

paragraphs: The Historical Marker Database records a monument on Broadway Street near North 6th Street in Thermopolis, in the median, at or near 527 Broadway Street. Photographs from June 4, 2016, show the marker on a statue titled From This Soil Come the Riches of the World, by Carl Jensen, 1999. The marker text says the statue depicts a cowboy sifting dirt through his hands in 1897, when Thermopolis was founded. It ties the soil to wildlife, the hot mineral water of Hot Springs State Park, oil, early coal, crops such as sugar beets, barley, alfalfa, and corn, and dinosaur fossils southeast of town.

The Thermopolis Independent Record, on May 26, 2022, shows volunteers repainting the brand tiles on the Pioneer Cowboy and Horse statue downtown. It says the statue is dedicated to the first 100 years of Thermopolis history, 1897 to 1997. That local name, Pioneer Cowboy and Horse, is the same downtown monument the marker page photographs.

Weights for the horse and the man, and a count of ranch brands, appear in an older travel blog that was not opened. Those numbers are not used. The marker page is the source for the artist, the year, the title, the pose, and the Broadway location.
